prompt: Each claim that X causes Y has a weakness. Name the condition for causality that it fails to satisfy.

cases.text: A brand manager credits a new jingle for sales, yet weeks with and without the jingle on air show the same sales.
cases.explanation: The presumed cause and the presumed effect do not vary together, so the first condition fails.

cases.text: Stores that gave a snack more shelf space sell more of it, but managers added the space after noticing the snack was selling well.
cases.explanation: The higher sales came before the extra shelf space, so the presumed cause does not precede the effect.

cases.text: A bakery's sales rose after it installed a new sign, but a large office building opened next door in the same month.
cases.explanation: The new office workers are another possible cause of the rise that has not been ruled out.

cases.text: Customers who received a discount email spent no more than customers who did not receive it.
cases.explanation: Receiving the email and spending do not vary together, so there is no association to explain.

cases.text: Gyms that advertise on radio have more members, but they are also the gyms located in the largest cities.
cases.explanation: City size could explain both the advertising and the membership, and it has not been ruled out.

cases.text: A café links its sales growth to a loyalty card, but the growth began two months before the card was introduced.
cases.explanation: The effect started before the presumed cause, so the time order condition fails.

prompt: Each case describes something that could distort the result of an experiment. Name the threat to internal validity.

cases.text: During a two-week test of a new cold-drink display, a heatwave raises drink sales across the whole city.
cases.explanation: An external event during the experiment affects the dependent variable.

cases.text: Over a six-month test of a new app feature, users become more skilled with the app and use it more, with or without the feature.
cases.explanation: The test units themselves change over time.

cases.text: Respondents who first answer a questionnaire about a brand pay closer attention to that brand when they later watch the test advertisement.
cases.explanation: The initial measurement influences the later measurement.

cases.text: Halfway through a checkout test, the analytics team starts counting a purchase only once payment has cleared.
cases.explanation: The measurement procedure, the definition of a conversion, changes during the test.

cases.text: Only managers who are enthusiastic about a new store layout agree to try it, and their stores were already outperforming the rest.
cases.explanation: The groups differed before the treatment because the stores volunteered.

cases.text: In a month-long taste test, participants who dislike the new recipe stop attending, while the control group stays complete.
cases.explanation: Test units leave at different rates across the groups.

prompt: Sort each study by the kind of experiment it is.

cards.text: Panel respondents view two versions of a shampoo advertisement in an online study and rate each one.
cards.explanation: An online study with a panel of respondents is an artificial environment constructed by the researcher.

cards.text: A supermarket chain changes the shelf price of a yogurt in 40 of its stores and compares weekly sales with its other stores.
cards.explanation: Behavior is observed in actual stores under real conditions.

cards.text: Participants shop in a simulated store built inside a research facility.
cards.explanation: A simulated store is an artificial setting that gives strong control over extraneous variables.

cards.text: An airline shows two fare displays to real customers on its live booking website.
cards.explanation: A live website is a natural setting, and customers may be unaware of the experiment.

cards.text: Participants at a research center taste three unbranded colas under identical lighting and rate them.
cards.explanation: The researcher constructs and controls the setting.

cards.text: A bank mails two versions of a credit card offer to 20,000 customers and tracks applications.
cards.explanation: The offers reach customers in their ordinary circumstances, which supports external validity.

prompt: A streaming service wants to test a new sign-up page. Put the steps of the A/B test in order.

steps.text: State that the new page increases sign-ups, with sign-up rate as the primary metric.
steps.explanation: The hypothesis and the primary metric are specified first, before any data are collected.

steps.text: Calculate the visitors and days needed to detect the smallest lift worth acting on.
steps.explanation: Sample size and duration follow from the smallest effect of practical importance and the desired power.

steps.text: Set up random assignment of visitors to the current page or the new page.
steps.explanation: Random assignment is configured before the test starts.

steps.text: Run the test for three full weeks without checking early for significance.
steps.explanation: The test runs for its planned duration, across complete weekly cycles, without being stopped early.

steps.text: Test the difference in sign-up rate and report the lift with its confidence interval.
steps.explanation: The difference in the primary metric is tested, and the effect size and its interval are reported.

steps.text: Record the decision and its reasons, even if the difference was not significant.
steps.explanation: The decision and rationale are documented, including tests with no significant difference.

question_text: A coffee chain renovates its stores in City X but not in City Y. Average daily customers per store rise from 400 to 460 in City X and from 420 to 440 in City Y over the same period. What is the difference-in-differences estimate of the renovation's effect?
hint: Compute each city's change first, then compare the two changes.

options.option_explanation: This is City X's change alone (460 − 400), a before–after comparison that ignores what happened in City Y over the same period.
This compares the two cities after the renovation only (460 − 440), ignoring that they started from different levels.
Correct. City X changed by 60 and City Y by 20; the difference between the two changes is 60 − 20 = 40.
This adds the two changes instead of subtracting the control city's change from the treated city's change.

prompt: A team plans an experiment on an eco-label for a detergent package. Sort each question by what can answer it.

bins.label: A pilot with simulated subjects can check this
Only real participants can establish this

cards.text: Whether the instructions to participants are clear.
cards.explanation: Pilots with simulated subjects can reveal unclear instructions.

cards.text: Whether the labelled and unlabelled packages look different enough to convey the treatment.
cards.explanation: Pilots can reveal stimuli that fail to convey the intended difference.

cards.text: Whether the question asking which package participants saw works as a manipulation check.
cards.explanation: Pilots can reveal manipulation checks that do not work.

cards.text: How much the eco-label raises consumers' purchase intention.
cards.explanation: The responses of simulated subjects are not evidence of how consumers respond, and the materials may lead the model to exaggerate the effect.

cards.text: Whether the effect of the label is larger among older consumers.
cards.explanation: How actual consumer groups respond can be established only with real participants.

cards.text: Whether the label increases the detergent's sales.
cards.explanation: A pilot precedes an experiment with real participants and does not replace it.

prompt: Sort each situation by the approach that suits its objective.

cards.text: A news site chooses among four headlines for a story that will be read mostly in the next six hours.
cards.explanation: The objective is to maximize performance during a short period.

cards.text: A retailer needs to know how much a free-shipping threshold raises average order value, for next year's plan.
cards.explanation: An accurate estimate of the size of an effect calls for a fixed A/B test.

cards.text: A three-day flash sale must show the best-performing banner as quickly as possible.
cards.explanation: A short promotion benefits from exposing fewer users to inferior versions.

cards.text: A product team wants to understand why a redesigned checkout performs better before rolling it out worldwide.
cards.explanation: Understanding why one version performs better calls for a fixed A/B test.

cards.text: An email campaign for a weekend event chooses among five subject lines while the campaign runs.
cards.explanation: Performance matters only during the short campaign, so reducing exposure to weaker versions is the priority.

cards.text: A subscription service must report the effect of a price change, with a confidence interval, to its board.
cards.explanation: A bandit's unequal, changing allocation does not support the same statistical inferences as a fixed test.

prompt: A researcher studies AI agents that book hotels. Match each manipulated factor with its example.

pairs.match: The agent is told that it works for the booking platform rather than for the traveler.
pairs.explanation: The system prompt sets the party the agent is told it serves.

pairs.match: The request reads "find me a good hotel" in one condition and "find the hotel with the lowest total price for three nights" in the other.
pairs.explanation: The consumer's instruction varies in the specificity of the goal.

pairs.match: Checking each hotel's cancellation policy costs the agent a tool call priced at $5.
pairs.explanation: The information environment sets the cost of acquiring an attribute.

pairs.match: One of the hotels on the list carries a "Sponsored" label.
pairs.explanation: A sponsorship label is an attribute of one of the alternatives.

prompt: Each record of tool calls ends in a poor choice. Name the source of the poor choice.

cases.text: The agent opens only the prices of two detergents, never the number of loads, and picks the cheaper bottle, which costs more per load.
cases.explanation: The information needed for the right choice was never acquired; given what it saw, picking the cheaper bottle was consistent.

cases.text: The agent opens the price and size of both cereals, computes the price per gram incorrectly and picks the one that costs more per gram.
cases.explanation: The necessary information was acquired but used incorrectly.

cases.text: The agent opens the unit price of both options, states that B is cheaper per unit, and then chooses A.
cases.explanation: The agent had the information and stated the right conclusion, but its choice did not follow from it.

cases.text: Told that each inspection costs $10, the agent opens a single cell and chooses immediately.
cases.explanation: The agent stopped searching before it had the attributes needed to compare the options.

cases.text: Asked for the best deal on coffee, the agent opens the brand and the rating of each coffee but none of the prices.
cases.explanation: The attributes that define a good deal were omitted before choosing.

cases.text: The agent opens every attribute of three laptops and then chooses the one that is worst on the goal it was given.
cases.explanation: All the information was acquired; the poor choice arose from how it was used.
